title: "Universal Differential Equations"
subtitle: "Discovering an unknown elimination process with a hybrid ODE + neural network"

In a standard deep compartment model the neural network predicts the *parameters* of
an ODE. In a **universal differential equation** (UDE) the neural network is *part of
the ODE*: it replaces a term of the right-hand side that is not known. For the models
in this package that right-hand side is

```
dA/dt = [I, 0, ..., 0] + NN(A; θ)
```

where `I` is the infusion rate that the dosing callback sets for the individual, and
the network learns the remaining dynamics from the data. This tutorial simulates a
drug with saturable (Michaelis-Menten) elimination and learns the elimination curve
from amount-time data.

## Setup

```{julia}
using DeepCompartmentModels   # also re-exports Lux, Optimisers, OrdinaryDiffEq, ...
using CairoMakie
using Random
```

## Simulate data

The true system is a single compartment, in amounts, with Michaelis-Menten elimination:
`dA/dt = I - Vmax * A / (Km + A)`. Every subject gets a different dose, which makes
the amounts cover a wide range. The dosing callback is the same object that is later
used for fitting. Note that the solver has to stop at the callback times (`tstops`),
otherwise the infusion is never switched off.

```{julia}
function true_ode!(dA, A, p, t)
    Vmax, Km, I = p
    dA[1] = I - Vmax * A[1] / (Km + A[1])
end

rng = Random.Xoshiro(1)
t_obs = Float32[0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24]

population = Population(map(1:12) do i
    dose = Float32(50 + 25 * (i % 4))
    callback = generate_dosing_callback(Float32[0 dose], Float32)

    prob = ODEProblem(true_ode!, Float32[0], (-0.1f0, 24f0), Float32[8, 20, 0])
    sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(); callback, saveat = t_obs, tstops = callback.condition.times)
    y = max.(only.(sol.u) .+ 0.5f0 .* randn(rng, Float32, length(t_obs)), 0f0)

    Individual(i, Float32[1], t_obs, y, callback, Float32)
end)
```

## Define the UDE

A `UniversalDiffEq` holds the structure of the ODE; the network goes in the
`DeepCompartmentModel`. `UniversalDiffEq(1)` is a system with a single state. The
network takes the state as its input and returns the rate of change that is not
accounted for by the dose. Because that is the *elimination*, the network has to learn
a negative number, so its last layer has no activation function.

```{julia}
ude = UniversalDiffEq(1)

nn = Lux.Chain(
    Lux.Dense(1, 16, tanh),
    Lux.Dense(16, 16, tanh),
    Lux.Dense(16, 1),
)

dcm = DeepCompartmentModel(ude, nn)
```

::: {.callout-note}
The `sensealg` of the model decides how gradients are propagated through the ODE
solver. For small networks (fewer than ~250 parameters) forward-mode sensitivities
(`ForwardDiffSensitivity`) are fastest; for larger networks an adjoint method scales
better. `DeepCompartmentModel` picks `GaussAdjoint(; autojacvec = ReverseDiffVJP(true))`
for larger UDEs, and you can always pass your own with `sensealg = ...`. The compiled
`ReverseDiffVJP(true)` is only valid when the right-hand side has no branches that
depend on the values of the states or parameters.
:::

## Initialise and fit

`setup` creates the parameters `ps` and the (Lux) state `st`. For a UDE the network
weights live in `ps.theta`, together with the infusion rate `I`, which the dosing
callback manages (it is never trained).

```{julia}
obj = SSE()
ps, st = setup(obj, rng, dcm)
keys(ps.theta)
```

`fit` minimises the objective with an Optimisers.jl rule. It returns the optimiser state, the
trained parameters and the state, and calls `callback(epoch, loss)` every epoch.
`parallel = :individual` solves the individuals on separate threads (start Julia with `-t auto`
to benefit).

```{julia}
losses = Float32[]
opt_state, ps, st = fit(obj, dcm, population, Optimisers.Adam(3f-3), ps, st;
    epochs = 800,
    parallel = :individual,
    callback = (epoch, loss) -> push!(losses, loss),
)

println("SSE: ", round(first(losses), digits = 1), " -> ", round(last(losses), digits = 1))
```

`fit` is a thin wrapper, there is no hidden magic. The call above is equivalent to this loop,
which you can use directly if you need more control (for example custom learning rate schedules,
early stopping or extra logging):

```{julia}
#| eval: false
opt_state = Optimisers.setup(Optimisers.Adam(3f-3), ps)

for epoch in 1:800
    ∇ = gradient(obj, dcm, population, ps, st; parallel = :individual)   # gradient of the objective w.r.t. ps
    opt_state, ps = Optimisers.update(opt_state, ps, ∇)                  # one optimiser step
end
```

```{julia}
fig = Figure(size = (600, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Epoch", ylabel = "SSE", yscale = log10)
lines!(ax, losses)
fig
```

## Predictions

`predict` solves the UDE for an individual (or a population) and returns the
predicted observations. Pass `saveat` for a dense time grid.

```{julia}
t_grid = collect(0f0:0.25f0:24f0)

fig = Figure(size = (800, 500))
for (i, indv) in enumerate(population[1:4])
    row, col = divrem(i - 1, 2)
    ax = Axis(fig[row + 1, col + 1]; title = "Subject $(indv.id)", xlabel = "Time (h)", ylabel = "Amount")
    scatter!(ax, get_t(indv), get_y(indv); color = :black)
    lines!(ax, t_grid, predict(dcm, indv, ps, st; saveat = t_grid))
end
fig
```

## Inspect the learned elimination

Since the network is the elimination term, we can evaluate it directly and compare it
to the truth. `Lux.StatefulLuxLayer` binds the state of the network so that it can be
called as a function of the input and the parameters.

```{julia}
nn_fit = Lux.StatefulLuxLayer{true}(nn, nothing, st.theta)

amounts = collect(0f0:1f0:100f0)
learned = -vec(nn_fit(reshape(amounts, 1, :), ps.theta))
truth = @. 8f0 * amounts / (20f0 + amounts)

fig = Figure(size = (500, 350))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Amount A (mg)", ylabel = "Elimination rate (mg/h)")
lines!(ax, amounts, learned; label = "Neural network")
lines!(ax, amounts, truth; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "True (Michaelis-Menten)")
axislegend(ax; position = :rb)
fig
```

After 800 epochs the network follows the saturating shape and is close to the truth at
high amounts, but it is still off at low amounts (below ~30 mg), and the SSE is still
well above the noise level of the simulation. Training for longer brings the curves closer
together. Outside the range of amounts that occur in the data, for example close to
zero, the network extrapolates and should not be trusted.

::: {.callout-note}
In this model the network is shared by everyone: there are no individual parameters or
random effects inside the ODE. All subjects therefore have the same elimination curve,
which is why the simulated subjects here differ only in their dose.
:::

## Summary

- `UniversalDiffEq(n)` + a Lux network in `DeepCompartmentModel` gives a hybrid ODE in
  which the network learns the dynamics that are not known.
- `setup`, `fit`, `gradient`, `predict` and the objectives (`SSE`, `MSE`, `LogLikelihood`) work as for any
  other model in the package; the weights live in `ps.theta`.
- Use `type = TimeConcatUDE()` to give the network the time as an extra input, and
  `inplace = true` for an in-place right-hand side.
